items.title: Treasury yields move higher as investors assess U.S. inflation backdrop
items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Monday as investors continue to weigh the domestic inflation and interest rate backdrop against broader geopolitical developments. The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose more than 4 basis points to 5.146%. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist bond yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.478%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was up more than 3 basis points at 4.772%. ... The moves come as inflation concerns continue to loom over the U.S. economy. Last week's strong inflation data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics saw wholesale prices rise 6.3% annually last month — the biggest jump since 2022 — with consumer costs up 3.7% annually in September, beating estimates. Meanwhile, U.S. crude prices rose Monday as investors continued to weigh tensions in the Middle East, as well as those between Russia and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for November delivery were up 2.22% to close at $103.66 per barrel. Brent crude Add To Watchlist, the global oil price benchmark, dropped 0.28% to $109.55, however. With the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision due Oct. 28, traders are now pricing in an above-80% probability that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will leave borrowing costs unchanged, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a ... The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target. ... Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%. Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year. ... By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks. ... Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago. ... The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones. ... Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.

items.title: Hassett Says CPI Data Shows Inflation Needs ‘Some Work’
items.excerpt: Enda Curran Mon, October 19, 2026 at 5:04 PM GMT+3 2 min read ... (Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said prices have been falling for items such as beef and eggs, though consumer price data for September shows overall inflation continues to need policy attention. "If you look at the previous three months, it looked like inflation was completely under control, and now it looks like it's sort of back needing some work," Hassett told CNBC Monday. Data last week showed consumer prices advanced in September at the fastest pace in five months and a gauge of underlying price pressures rose by more than expected. The consumer price index rose 0.6% from a month earlier while a key measure of underlying price pressures, which excludes food and energy, was up 0.3%. "This is either a sort of break from the downtrend or a blip," Hassett said in the interview. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh last week did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month. In a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. Hassett said he respects the central bank's independence and said Warsh will "do what he thinks is the right thing." ... "People are really euphoric about how well the economy is doing, and they're spending more. And of course, that's the kind of thing the Fed needs to pay attention to," Hassett said.

items.excerpt: Headlines for October 19, 2026 | Democracy Now! ## Hundreds of Thousands March in Over 140 Cities in France on Saturday Oct 19, 2026 In France, hundreds of thousands of protesters marched in over 140 cities on Saturday, demanding relief from the high cost of living, more funding for public services and improvements to deteriorating schools, among other grievances. The demonstrations were the latest — and largest — in a series of protests that began in September with student-led rallies over overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure, that have since grown to a broader nationwide movement. Some cities saw property destruction, arson and theft, with isolated incidents of violence. There was damage reported to symbols of the state, including city halls in Lille, Marseille and Limoges, and a tourist office in Lyon. Officials said almost 1,000 police officers were injured, and some 2,400 people were arrested. France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police had “lost control,” and offered to resign. President Emmanuel Macron rejected his offer.
